sources.citation: 塚本晃久 [Tsukamoto, Akihisa]. 2019. 孤島での苦難 ― トンガ王国タファヒ島の民話 [Sufferings on an isolated island: folktales from Tafahi, the Kingdom of Tonga]. 南半球評論 (The Southern Hemisphere Review, ANZ Literary Society of Japan) 35: 21-32. DOI 10.20743/anzshr.35.0_21.
sources.note: Nothing. Full text extracted (extracted text, 527 lines) and searched for アクセント / 強勢 / ストレス / 声調 / stress / accent / tone: zero hits. Only phonological remark is a transcription note (p. 22) on rendering Tongan glottal stop and velar nasal in katakana. The Tongan text carries standard orthographic definitive-accent marks, which concern Tongan, not the 1616 language.
sources.venue: 南半球評論 (The Southern Hemisphere Review, ANZ Literary Society of Japan)

sources.citation: Glottolog 5.1 languoid page niua1241 (and local hh.bib entries citing Niuatoputapu [nkp]).
sources.note: No descriptive references at all; only wordlist re-editions (Relandus 1708, Richer 1777, Kern 1948) and Biggs 1971 for subclassification. Status extinct.

sources.citation: Wikipedia (English). 'Tafahi' (island article), section 'Language' and References. Raw wikitext downloaded 2026-09-21.
sources.note: Nothing on stress, accent or tone (a full-text search for stress/accent the wikitext: no such words).

sources.citation: Wikipedia. Niuatoputapu language (English article, raw wikitext downloaded 2026-09-17).
sources.note: Nothing. Phonology sketch (5 vowels short/long, 10 consonants, possible glottal stop) derived from the 32-word Le Maire list; no stress statement.

sources.citation: Marck, Jeff. 2000. Topics in Polynesian language and culture history. Pacific Linguistics 504. Canberra: Pacific Linguistics, ANU.
sources.note: Discusses stress only for Proto-Polynesian (ch. 3: 'Polynesian languages usually have penultimate stress which was certainly a feature of Proto Polynesian'; Table 3.2 generalised PPn word stress). Niuatoputapu occurs only in the abbreviation list (Ntu) and one geographic sentence on p. 17; no Niuatoputapu data or stress statement.

sources.citation: Jonsson, Niklas (transcriber/editor). n.d. [c. 1998]. The Niuatoputapu wordlist by Jacob Le Maire. POLLInet texts (Language: Niuatoputapu), Department of Linguistics, Stockholm University. Internet Archive copy 2022-12-09.
sources.note: Wordlist-only data (5 items, no accent marks); no statement about stress, accent or tone; the words 'stress'/'accent' do not occur.

sources.citation: Jonsson, Niklas. 1998. Niuatoputapu: language facts sheet. POLLInet (Stockholm University), data last updated 16 Dec 1998.
sources.note: Nothing. States the language is extinct, 'known from a few words collected by Le Maire in the 17th century', gives a letter list from Biggs (1971: 491) and a bibliography (Biggs 1971, Dye 1983, Kern 1948, Kirch 1988, Rogers 1973/1975, Schouten 1619).

sources.citation: Dye, T. S. 1980. The linguistic position of Niuafo'ou. Journal of the Polynesian Society 89(3): 349-358.
sources.note: Nothing. The article is about Niuafo'ou (not Niuatoputapu; the earlier scan's title was wrong). Its PHONOLOGY section (pp. 349-351) covers PPN consonant/vowel correspondences only; Niuatoputapu (NTU) is named on pp. 352-353: 'Recent TON borrowing has left Niuatoputapu (NTU) indistinguishable from TON, though the inhabitants spoke a distinctly non-TON language in 1616 when Jacob LeMaire collected a word list there (Biggs 1971: 491).' No word 'stress' or 'accent' anywhere in the text.

sources.citation: de Villiers, J. A. J. (ed. and transl.). 1906. Works issued by the Hakluyt Society, 2nd series, 18. London: Hakluyt Society.
sources.note: Nothing: voyage narrative of the encounter (trade, skirmish, canoes); no vocabulary and no remark on the language (a full-text search for stress/accent vocabular/language/tongue/accent: no hits in these pages).
sources.venue: Works issued by the Hakluyt Society, 2nd series

sources.citation: Le Maire, Jacob. 1622. Spieghel der Australische navigatie (with 'Vocabulaer oft tale van d'eylanden Salomonis'). Amsterdam. Images at David Rumsey Map Collection.
sources.note: The original 32-word list; the sole attestation of the language. Orthographic Dutch transcription without stress marking.
